text: The Sun now slides across the sky about its own width every minute.
That is as fast as the hour hand on a clock.
Night is only six hours long, too.
Eight hours of sleep no longer fits inside one night.
A year now holds about seven hundred and thirty days.
Storms are steered twice as hard as today.
Nothing here would feel dangerous yet, only strange.
That is about sixteen hundred and seventy kilometers an hour.
The strongest gust ever measured on Earth was about four hundred and eight kilometers an hour.
So this wind would be about four times stronger.
And it would blow from the east, because the ground is running ahead of the air.
Sand and dust would lift off the ground and race past in a flat, roaring sheet.
Slowly, friction would drag the air up to speed, over hours to days.
But in those first hours, anything loose, and plenty that is not, would be swept away.
Near the equator, the sea would creep far inland over the coasts.
Near the poles, the sea floor would be left bare.
Day and night each last three hours.
The sea at the equator now wants to stand about a hundred and sixty-five kilometers higher than it does today.
Again, that is only a rough guess.
It slides its own width every sixteen seconds.
The sea at the equator now wants to stand about seven hundred kilometers higher than it does today, another rough guess.
The same jump that lifts you half a meter today would now lift you about a meter.
Storms are steered twelve times harder than today, and a year holds more than four thousand days.
A seventy kilogram person would weigh about eight kilograms.
The same jump that lifts you half a meter today would carry you about four meters, higher than a basketball hoop.
A cup falling off a table would take about three times as long to land.
The Sun now crosses the whole sky in forty-five minutes.
It slides its own width every eight seconds.
Storms are steered sixteen times harder than today.
The sea at the equator now wants to stand about twenty-eight hundred kilometers higher than it does today. That is a rough guess, but it is hundreds of times the depth of the ocean.
A year now holds nearly six thousand days.
